name: Endpoint detection & response
summary: See and contain malicious activity on laptops, servers, and other endpoints.

controls.soc2: CC7.1 · Detection of changes and anomalies

soc2.ref: CC7.1 · Detection of changes and anomalies

practices.text: Every managed laptop and server reports to the console, and you reconcile that count against your asset list at least monthly.
Blocking is on in the standard policy, not detect-only, and every exception has an owner and a reason.
High-severity alerts are triaged within an agreed time, around the clock, by your team or a managed service.

claims.claim: Top results in MITRE ATT&CK Evaluations
claims.ask: Which steps were detected with the default configuration, without changes made during the test?

claims.claim: Autonomous or AI response, no analysts needed
claims.ask: Who investigates when the product is unsure, and how fast? Show a recent real case.

claims.claim: Lightweight agent with no performance impact
claims.ask: Show CPU, memory, and crash data for the operating systems you run, including Linux and macOS.

proof: A proof of concept on your own device builds, in blocking mode, with your own test techniques (for example Atomic Red Team).
The managed service's response-time commitment and a sanitised sample incident report.
What raw telemetry you can export to your SIEM, and whether that costs extra.
redFlags: You are not allowed to run your own tests during the trial.
Pricing depends on a multi-year commitment before you have tested it.
Telemetry stays locked in their console unless you buy a higher tier.

name: Security monitoring
summary: Collect logs and investigate detections across the estate.

practices.text: Identity, endpoint, email, cloud control-plane, and network logs all arrive, and a source that goes quiet raises an alert.
Detections are mapped to MITRE ATT&CK and tested at least quarterly, for example with adversary emulation.
Logs are kept as long as your frameworks require, and investigations follow a written runbook.

claims.ask: Quote the cost at your current log volume and at double it, including retention and search.

claims.claim: Hundreds of detections out of the box
claims.ask: How many fire usefully on your data, and how many need tuning first?
On whose data, measured how, and what does the AI do when it is wrong?

proof: Parsers for your top ten log sources working in the trial, not on the roadmap.
Detections firing on your own test activity, with the false-positive rate over two weeks.
How you get your data and detection content out if you leave, in what format, and at what cost.
redFlags: Only ingest is quoted; search, long retention, or detections are sold separately.
Detection content cannot be exported or managed as code.
Key log sources need professional services to onboard.

name: Identity & access
summary: Authenticate people, gate privileged access, and retire stale accounts.

pci.ref: 8 · Identify users and authenticate access, incl. MFA (8.4)

practices.text: MFA is enforced for every user, and administrators use phishing-resistant methods such as FIDO2 keys or passkeys.
Admin work uses separate accounts with time-bound or approved access, not everyday accounts.
Joiners, movers, and leavers are driven from HR, and privileged and critical-app access is reviewed at least quarterly.

claims.ask: What happens when a user loses their only device? Show the recovery flow.
Which device, network, and app signals does a sign-in decision actually use?
Which of your top 20 apps support SSO and automatic provisioning, and on which tier?

proof: Phishing-resistant MFA options and how enrolment works for your workforce.
How the vendor protects its own admin access, and its public incident history.
Licence tiers needed for conditional access, governance, and privileged access.
redFlags: SSO or provisioning is held back for an enterprise-only tier that was not disclosed upfront.
No documented break-glass process.
Vague answers about the vendor's own past breaches.

name: Email security
summary: Stop phishing, malware, and impersonation before the inbox.

controls.cis: CIS 9 · Email and web browser protections

cis.ref: CIS 9 · Email and web browser protections

practices.text: Every sending domain has SPF, DKIM, and DMARC at quarantine or reject.
Staff have a report button, and reported mail is triaged and pulled from other inboxes.
Attachments are sandboxed and links are checked at the time of click.

claims.ask: Of what sample, and what does it miss? Run it against your own mail.
Show the BEC messages it would have flagged from your last 90 days.
What is the false-positive rate, and who releases quarantined mail?

proof: A retro-scan of 30 to 90 days of your mail, showing what it caught that your current filter missed, message by message.
Whether it works by API or needs an MX change, and what happens to mail if the service is down.
How it handles the protection already in your Microsoft 365 or Google Workspace licence.
redFlags: Retro-scan results shown only as totals, never individual messages.
An MX change with no failover plan.
Claims that it removes the need for SPF, DKIM, and DMARC.

name: Backup & recovery
summary: Keep restorable copies so ransomware is not the only copy of the data.

practices.text: Critical systems have an immutable or offline copy that a compromised admin account cannot delete.
A full restore of a critical system is tested at least twice a year and meets the agreed recovery time.
Backup consoles use separate credentials with MFA, not domain admin accounts.

claims.ask: Can an administrator, or the vendor's support team, shorten retention or delete a copy?
Walk through a scenario where an attacker holds domain admin. What still survives?
Time a restore of a system your size during the trial.

proof: How immutability is enforced: storage lock, separate account, or only a setting.
Measured restore throughput for your data volume, not best-case figures.
Every fee in a restore: egress, recovery, or professional services.
redFlags: Immutability is a policy setting a compromised admin can switch off.
Restore testing is a paid extra.
Egress or recovery fees are left out of the quote.

name: Vulnerability management
summary: Find exposed weaknesses and drive them to a patch or a compensating control.

practices.text: Scans cover endpoints, servers, cloud, and the external perimeter at least weekly, authenticated where possible.
Fix times are set by risk, for example known-exploited vulnerabilities within 14 days, and are measured.
Every exception has an owner, a compensating control, and an expiry date.

claims.ask: How many assets did discovery find in the trial compared with your asset list?
Which inputs drive the score (CISA KEV, EPSS, exploit code, asset value), and can you see them?
What is missed without credentials or an agent?

proof: Authenticated scan coverage on your operating systems and cloud services.
An API that exports every finding, with fix status.
How short-lived cloud assets are counted for licensing.
redFlags: The priority score is a black box.
Per-IP licensing that quietly penalises autoscaling.
Findings cannot be exported in bulk.

name: Cloud security posture
summary: Watch configuration, identity, and workload risk in public cloud.

controls.cis: CIS 4 · Secure configuration of enterprise assets

cis.ref: CIS 4 · Secure configuration of enterprise assets

practices.text: Every cloud account and subscription is connected automatically, including new ones.
Critical misconfigurations such as public storage or exposed admin ports alert an owner and are fixed within an agreed time.
Preventive guardrails (for example AWS SCPs, Azure Policy, or GCP organization policies) block the most dangerous settings instead of only reporting them.

claims.ask: What permissions does it need, and is any of it write access?
Show feature parity for AWS, Azure, and GCP for the services you actually use.
Show three real attack paths from your account and how you would fix each.

proof: Connect a real account in the trial and review the top ten findings with your engineers.
How it reaches your ticketing system and your infrastructure-as-code pipeline.
How workloads are counted for pricing when you autoscale.
redFlags: Write permissions required for basic posture checks.
Success measured by the number of findings, not risk reduced.
Pricing per workload that is not explained for autoscaling.

name: Secure web access
summary: Inspect web traffic and connect users to private apps without a flat network.

iso.ref: A.8.23 · Web filtering; A.8.20 · Network security

pci.ref: 1.3–1.4 · Restrict traffic to and from the CDE

practices.text: All managed devices send web traffic through it, on and off the office network.
Private apps are reached per app, not through a VPN onto a flat network.
TLS inspection is on for high-risk categories, with documented exceptions.

claims.ask: Which of your private apps and protocols work through it today, not only web apps?
Which user and device signals decide access to each app?
Measure latency from your users' locations in the trial.

proof: Points of presence near your users and where traffic is decrypted and logged.
How TLS inspection exceptions and certificate-pinned apps are handled.
Tested compatibility with your endpoint agent.
redFlags: You cannot choose the regions where your traffic is processed.
The client has not been tested alongside your endpoint agent.
The price is driven by bundled modules you will not use.

name: Web application testing
summary: Probe web apps the way an attacker would, request by request.

pci.ref: 6.4 · Protect public-facing web applications; 11.4 penetration testing

practices.text: Every internet-facing app is tested before major releases and at least once a year.
Testing is authenticated and covers access control and business logic, not only an unauthenticated scan.
Findings are tracked to a fix and retested, and fix times are measured.

claims.ask: Are findings verified by a person before they reach the report?
Which access control and business logic flaws did it find for a customer like you?
Which methodology (for example the OWASP Web Security Testing Guide), and what is out of scope?

proof: A sanitised report from a comparable engagement.
Named testers, their experience, and whether a retest is included.
How login, MFA, and single-page apps are handled.
redFlags: The report is mostly scanner output.
Retests cost extra.
The testers are not named or vetted.

name: Application security testing
summary: Catch vulnerable code, dependencies, containers, and IaC before release.

practices.text: Code, dependency, and secrets scanning run on every pull request for production code.
Critical findings block the build or need a recorded approval.
You keep an SBOM for each release and can find where a newly disclosed vulnerable library is used within a day.

claims.claim: Shift left with no developer friction
claims.ask: How long does a scan add to a pull request on a repo your size?
Run it on one of your real repos and count true and false findings.
Are the suggested fixes tested, and who reviews them?

proof: Languages and frameworks covered at full depth, not only syntax.
Exactly what is sent to the vendor's cloud, including source code, and how long it is kept.
How findings are de-duplicated across code, dependency, and container scans.
redFlags: Source code is uploaded without clear retention terms.
Per-developer pricing that counts every occasional committer.
Auto-fix pull requests that arrive without tests.

name: Adversary emulation
summary: Run small, repeatable attack techniques to see whether detections fire.

practices.text: A scheduled emulation plan is based on the threats that target your sector.
Each run records which detections fired, and every miss becomes a detection-engineering ticket.
Tests rerun after detection or tool changes to catch regressions.

claims.ask: How many techniques have working tests on each of your platforms?
How does each test clean up after itself?
Show a gap a customer found and the detection it led to.

proof: The list of implemented tests per platform.
Cleanup and rollback behaviour for each test.
Exportable results you can keep outside their console.
redFlags: Coverage counted by technique names, not working tests.
No cleanup or rollback.
Results can only be viewed in their console.

name: Security control validation
summary: Safely execute real attack paths to prove controls work in production.

practices.text: Validation runs in production at least monthly, not only in a lab.
Results are tracked over time per control: prevented, detected, or missed.
Failed controls have owners and are retested after the fix.

claims.ask: How often does it actually run in production, and what change approval does it need?
How are payloads made safe, and what happens if a test is interrupted?

claims.claim: Proves the value of your stack
claims.ask: Compare its results in the trial with what your SOC actually saw.

proof: Integrations with your EDR and SIEM that confirm detections automatically.
The evidence behind each pass or fail.
The rights its agents or accounts need.
redFlags: Scores shown without the evidence behind them.
Broad domain admin rights required.
The vendor also sells the products it recommends replacing yours with.

name: Security awareness
summary: Train people to spot phishing and report it without slowing the business.

controls.cis: CIS 14 · Security awareness and skills training

cis.ref: CIS 14 · Security awareness and skills training

practices.text: Everyone, including executives and contractors, is trained at hire and at least yearly.
Phishing simulations run at least quarterly, and you track how many people report them, not only who clicks.
High-risk roles such as finance, administrators, developers, and the help desk get training for their role.

claims.ask: Measured how, on what population, over what period?
Show completion rates and module length from a customer your size.
What data about staff does the personalisation use?

proof: Sample training content and how long each module takes.
Report-rate and repeat-clicker trends from a comparable customer.
How simulations respect HR and works-council rules.
redFlags: Click rate is the only metric.
Simulations that fake bonuses or pay changes in ways that damage trust.
Basic content is locked behind higher tiers.

name: Compliance automation
summary: Map evidence to frameworks so audits are a readout, not a fire drill.

controls.iso: A.5.36 · Compliance with policies and standards

iso.ref: A.5.36 · Compliance with policies and standards

practices.text: Evidence for technical controls is collected from your systems through integrations, not screenshots.
A failing control alerts its owner and is tracked to closure.
One set of controls is mapped to all your frameworks, so each control is tested once.

claims.ask: How long did it take a customer with your stack and frameworks?
Which of your controls are collected automatically and which are uploaded by hand?
How is the auditor's independence from the platform protected?

proof: Integrations for the systems you actually run.
Export of all evidence and policies in open formats.
How one control is mapped across your frameworks.
redFlags: An auditor paid through the platform with no independence safeguards.
Template policies that are not tailored to how you work.
Evidence locked in the platform with no export.

name: Risk & IRM
summary: Run policies, risks, and audit findings as one program of record.

controls.cis: CIS Controls · Governance and risk overlay

cis.ref: No CIS safeguard; CIS assumes a risk process exists

practices.text: A risk register with owners, ratings, and treatment decisions is reviewed by leadership at least quarterly.
Policies have owners and review dates, and staff acknowledge them.
Audit findings and exceptions are tracked to closure with due dates.

claims.ask: Which modules do you need for your use case, and what does each cost?
How long and how much did implementation cost a customer your size?
Can you explain each score to an auditor?

proof: Implementation time, partner costs, and admin skills needed.
How workflows are changed and by whom.
Data export formats if you leave.
redFlags: An implementation partner is required but not in the quote.
Basic features are split into separately licensed modules.
Risk scores you cannot explain to your auditors.
